title: Treating chronic back pain: partial recovery
description: Long-lasting pain is linked with less grey matter in parts of the brain. This study asked whether that reverses when the pain is treated. People with chronic low back pain were scanned before and six months after spine surgery or joint injections. In those who improved, the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which had been thinner than in people without pain, became thicker, and its activity during an attention task returned to normal. Other thinner areas stayed thinner. In this episode brightness stands for cortical thickness, not activity. In the first part it shows the difference from people without pain; in "What changed" it shows the change since before treatment.
caveat: This is one study: 18 patients and 16 people without pain were compared before treatment, and 14 patients were scanned again six months later. The thickening was significant only in the 11 who improved on pain or disability by any amount; across all 14 there was no significant change. Treatment was spine surgery or facet joint injections, so this shows pain relief in general, not one treatment, and the authors note a placebo effect may have contributed. Follow-up was six months. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.
